🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

In politics, memories can be remarkably short. But North Carolinians should remember what happened in the spring of 2020.

During COVID-19, Gov. Roy Cooper issued Executive Order 138. Under his administration’s guidance, indoor worship services were generally limited to ten people, while gatherings of more than ten worshipers were directed outdoors unless meeting outside was “impossible.”

At the same time, many retail businesses were permitted to operate indoors at up to 50 percent of their fire-code capacity. Funerals could include as many as 50 people.

Churches objected. Pastors sued.

And on May 16, 2020, U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III issued a temporary restraining order preventing enforcement of those worship restrictions.

The court concluded that the churches had demonstrated they were likely to succeed on their claim that the restrictions violated the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment.

Judge Dever wrote words worth remembering: “There is no pandemic exception to the Constitution of the United States or the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment.”

The court also highlighted the unequal treatment created by the order. Cooper’s own attorney conceded during the hearing that there was no public-health rationale for permitting 50 people indoors at a funeral while generally restricting indoor religious worship to ten.

Cooper defended his policy on public-health grounds, arguing that people sitting together indoors for extended periods presented greater transmission risks than shoppers moving through a store. After the federal court intervened, however, Cooper announced that his administration would not appeal.

North Carolinians can debate the difficult decisions made during an unprecedented pandemic.

But we should not rewrite history.

When government power expanded during a crisis, churches in North Carolina had to go to federal court to protect their ability to gather for worship.

That record deserves to be remembered.

Sources: Berean Baptist Church v. Cooper, U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina, May 16, 2020; WRAL, “Federal judge allows NC churches to meet inside,” May 16, 2020; WRAL/PolitiFact, “Fact check: Cooper claim about churches and retail shops,” May 29, 2020.The underlying federal ruling is particularly strong sourcing: it documents the 10-person rule, the “outdoors unless impossible” provision, the 50-person funeral exception, and the court’s Free Exercise analysis.

text:
grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. “Meta plugged its API into Sahyog so posts vanish with no human review” mixes up two completely different systems.

“When I was pregnant with you I was under pressure to have an abortion but I refused. I chose instead to bring you into this world.” 

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..now Coming out later in Dec 2025. Give me some feedback. 

My mother did not hesitate to bring up the circumstances around my birth and conception every time I tried her patience as a young boy. Granted, she always told me she loved me, but I got to know my chequered history quite early. “Your father’s parents owned a shop and the women who worked there assured me that it was unacceptable and totally reprehensible, a taboo, for an African woman and an Asian man to get together, let alone produce a child from that union. The only solution they said, was to perform an abortion and end that life before it even began. But I refused!" 

I was conceived towards the end of the 60s, a few years into Uganda’s journey as an independent country, a few years before Idi Amin Dada started his rule in Uganda. I am told it was the time of miniskirts and twist dancing in Uganda, and the time of the American sex revolution! My father was a young Asian of (most likely) Indian descent whose family was one of the trading families in Masaka. 

He was a student at Makerere University, and that is the extent of my knowledge about my father. Soon after I was born, President Iddi Amin declared an economic war of indigenization and my father was among those who were deported/expelled out of Uganda. The History of Uganda is such that Asians, particularly Indians took the lion’s share of trading licences. President Amin wanted to reverse this unfair advantage but unfortunately, it meant I would never get to meet my father or his family. Not only was I born in a conflicted relationship of races, I never got a chance to know who my father was, nor his family. Despite the great love and acceptance that I received from my mother, siblings and my Baganda tribal family, I always felt a great sense of “father hunger” - that yearning for fatherly protection, provision and affirmation which only a Dad could provide. 

My mother was a primary school teacher who was struggling to raise eight children as a single parent. She had been married to James Kyeyune, a medical officer and they were blessed with six children but their marriage broke down. My mother always told me that she could not accept being a co-wife. My step father had brought another wife home and she could not accept the idea of sharing a husband. Despite the efforts of the good catholic bishops who intervened to smooth things over, the marriage broke down and she moved away in the mid-60s to start a new life as a teacher and a single mother. I was born into a family of seven other children, five boys and two girls. Dickson, the eldest had gone off to join the police force, Joseph the second born and Edward the fifth born stayed with their paternal grandparents. Clare and Fred were students in a Catholic boarding school and came home only during the holidays. This meant that the three youngest children Florence, John and myself were the ones who stayed home with mother. 

Owing to my bi-racial parentage, my looks were quite different from the rest of the family and the children around me. I had big curly hair unlike my brother’s kinky hair. I had much lighter skin due to my father’s suspected Asian descent. In our Baganda culture, the name of a child is based on the clan of the father and in the absence of my biological father, my mother gave me the names of her father, Ssempa which meant that I belonged to my mother’s clan; symbolically represented by the colobus monkey (Nkima). My grandfather, Alipo Ssempa was an educated British colonial government administrator and interpreter in Masaka. Sadly, I never got to meet him as death took him before we could meet. His father, Bisakka or Bishaka who was my great grandfather had been a noteworthy regional trader in the Buganda, Ankole, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Tanzania region. 

He was called Bisaka, a name very closely related to Kisaka which is a large cluster or collection of trees and bushes which occurs on the savannah plains and hills in this region. It’s like an individual collection of a family of trees and bushes which are separated from others by savannah grass fields. Just as his name implies, my great grandfather had eighty wives which made up his large family! Bisaka was known as Bishaka by the western Ankole-Rwanda tribes whose language is characterized by the ‘sh’ making him multi tribal/multi lingual and multi-wifey. Unfortunately, this great trader and lover of the sweet affections of the beautiful women of Buganda, Ankole, Rwanda and Tanzania region suffered an early death which led to the scattering of the whole family. 

My great grandmother "Venecka Munaku Atambuza Mwoyo" [the poor walks guided by the spirit] and her sister who had also been a co-wife branched out Eastward and settled between Mityebiri/ Minziro in Rakai and Buyikuzi in Lukaya which is half way between Kampala city and Masaka town. Thus I carried the genes of Bisaka and the name of his son Ssempa, a fact which made people do a double take every time they met the bi-racial child with a native African name. It was not the norm. 

These bio-genetical differences were much more pronounced in my childhood. I stuck out both in the classroom and on the children’s playfield. I can compare it to being the only black student in an all-white students school or being the only white student at an all-black-African students school. To some, I was an object of curiosity and I often had to bear the discomfort of having my hair felt, so the kids with kinky hair could feel my curly hair. Most of them were kind, but others would mock me with unkind words, ”Ssempa was forgotten at the airport, the Indians forgot him with the suitcases and boxes at the airport.” They would laugh and others gave me the monicker, ‘Magoba ga Uganda’ a Luganda phrase meaning “Ugandan profit” which they would explain with youthful logic; “In the interaction between Uganda and India, Ssempa was the Ugandan profit.” These were painful words casually thrown around by some misguided youngsters. They did not reflect the sentiment of the whole Buganda community which accepted me as a son. But in the places where children interacted with minimal adult supervision; the classrooms, playing fields where adults were absent to guide, I was often called painful names, like ‘illegitimate,’ ‘bastard,’ ‘magoba ga Uganda.’ It is a fact of life that some children will mock those who are different or handicapped, maybe they have unusually large ears or nose. This is the foolishness of childhood which fortunately disappears as we grow older. 

Narozali is found in Buyange Parish, Kyanamukakaaka subcounty in Masaka district in the South West of Uganda. It was a large Roman catholic parish with a church, schools and many other projects run by the church. It was located about one hour from Masaka town, on the undulating hills surrounding the shores of Lake Victoria. My mother was a grade one (primary one) teacher at the parish and we stayed in a house provided by the school. My mother was a devout catholic and we attended daily morning mass as well as family evening prayers. We prayed much when there was trouble such as when there was war in the period of 1971-72. In 1971, the president of Uganda, Apollo Milton Obote was overthrown by his star General, Idi Amin Dada in a military takeover that changed Uganda’s political and economic terrain in which I was to grow up. First, the expulsion of Asians in his economic war policy of indigenization was a strange mixture of tragedy and triumph. It was tragic to the Indians whose families had built and run the back bone of the Ugandan economy and were unceremoniously expelled from the country. Most of all the industries, commercial farms, large and small trading shops were owned and run by Indian families who had the technical skills, experience and passion to operate them effectively. They were forced to vacate all of this in a short time not knowing where they were to go. The sudden loss of homes and wealth which had been accumulated for nearly a century led some unfortunate souls to suicides by the river Nile. Others travelled to Canada, England, Kenya and United States where they started a new life. Some ended up succeeding incredibly in their new homes, becoming the economic entrepreneurs of their new homelands. Soon after Idi Amin became president of Uganda, there was an ill-fated attempt to attack and militarily overthrow him by rebels based out of Tanzania. 

Our home of Narozali is in the South West region of Uganda’s territory next to Tanzania and at times, it seemed that we were living in a war zone. Military vehicles, jeeps and noisy Israeli-made warplanes above made it difficult to ignore the ongoing conflict. We spent a lot of time praying to God to intervene and even added special supplications to the Virgin Mary who had a special altar with her monument encased in a specially made grotto. Here we earnestly recited the rosary and asked for divine intervention. Providentially, the war ended soon as the attackers were defeated in a bloody massacre! The early efforts by the coalition of anti-Idi Amini forces to remove him militarily were unsuccessful and suffered huge casualties. For the natives, it was also a mixture of triumph and tragedy. Their struggle for independence from colonial masters had given them political gains without economic gains. The economy was controlled by the Indian merchant families giving little or no space for the emergence of African owned enterprises. This all changed suddenly as Iddi Amin began to apportion out enterprises to the natives. My mother applied to operate a stone quarry but was denied for some reason. However, native Ugandan's got to own and operate all sorts of businesses from industries to merchant shops. While it is true that many ended up being mismanaged and run into the ground, there were others which succeeded. The expulsion of the Asians/ Indians created a leadership vacuum which forced many Ugandans to quickly learn to trade in various enterprises, giving rise to Ugandan owned business. 

As a child of dual Asian-Ugandan ancestry, it was a loss for my father’s people, and a gain for my mother’s people. As Nyinamwiru, the daughter of Bukuku lamented when she learnt that her father had been killed by her son Karabumbi Nduhura who was now the new king, “My ears cause me to hear both evil and good, for is it not my son who has killed Bukuku? My father is dead, but my son reigns, thus I have sorrow on one arm but joy on the other.” This historical account of our ancestors’ dilemma describes my conflicted view of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Indians from Uganda. This view was later to be articulated in my college days by a professor of Political Science at Makerere University who said that Amin’s expulsion of Indians was the single most significant event in economic empowerment of the Ugandan natives. It was quite interesting because, Professor Mahmood Mamdani, was a Ugandan with Asian ancestry, just like me. To date, Uganda, unlike its East African counterparts Kenya and Tanzania has the greatest number of Africans who own business while the other two have businesses still largely owned by the original Asian families who had no Iddi Amin to shake them up. 

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..now Coming out later in Dec 2025

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
